narrative:
The model determined that you have a 69.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

Three factors drove this decision, ranked by importance. First, your LSAT score of 44 was the strongest influence, and it worked in your favor by pushing the prediction toward passing. Second, your first-year class ranking (bottom decile) was the next most important factor and strongly pushed the outcome toward failure. Third, your third-year class ranking (also bottom decile) added further weight toward failure.

In other words, although your LSAT performance was better than the average of students who were accepted, your consistently low class standing in both the first and third years of law school signaled a high risk that you would struggle to pass the bar. These academic performance signals outweighed the positive LSAT contribution.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking key courses to improve your class rank, enrolling in a structured bar-preparation program, or gaining additional practical legal experience before reapplying. These steps can directly address the factors that led to the rejection. (218 words)
